kurz: How capital losses are netted against gains, why only $3,000 a year can reduce other income, how the carryforward works and how the wash sale rule can wipe out a loss you were counting on.

bloecke.md:
A realized loss in a taxable account reduces your tax only within limits. Capital losses first offset capital gains of the same year, without any upper limit. If losses exceed gains, up to $3,000 of the net loss ($1,500 if married filing separately) can be deducted from other income such as wages or interest each year (26 U.S.C. § 1211(b)). The rest is carried forward to later years without a time limit (§ 1212(b)). Individuals cannot carry capital losses back to earlier years.

Many investors underestimate how slowly a large loss is used up without matching gains. A net loss of $30,000 in a year without gains takes ten years to deduct at $3,000 a year. Losses on personal-use property, such as your home or car, are not deductible at all.

Capital losses offset capital gains in full. Beyond that, at most $3,000 a year reduces other income. Any remaining loss is carried forward indefinitely; a carryback is not possible for individuals (26 U.S.C. §§ 1211(b) and 1212(b)).

Within capital gains and losses, there is a fixed order. Short-term gains and losses (holding period of one year or less) are netted against each other, and so are long-term gains and losses. If one group shows a net gain and the other a net loss, the two are then netted against each other. The character of what remains matters, because a net short-term gain is taxed at ordinary rates and a net long-term gain at 0%, 15% or 20%.

There are no separate pots for different kinds of securities. A loss on an individual stock offsets a gain on an ETF, a bond or a mutual fund, and the other way round. The netting is done on your return, on Form 8949 and Schedule D, across all your brokers. No broker needs to issue a special certificate for it; each one simply reports its sales on Form 1099-B.

bloecke.unter: Legal position in 2026 for individuals. A loss is used up in this order; whatever is left is carried forward with its short-term or long-term character.

bloecke.md: Two points are often misunderstood. First, a net capital loss does not wipe out qualified dividends. They are taxed at the preferential rates, and only the $3,000 deduction reduces your ordinary income. Second, if you have a loss carryforward, it is applied automatically to the next year's gains, even if those gains would have fallen into the 0% range anyway. You cannot save a carryforward for a year in which it would be worth more.

If you sell stock or securities at a loss and buy substantially identical stock or securities within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed (26 U.S.C. § 1091). The window covers 61 days in total. The disallowed loss is not lost for good: it is added to the basis of the new shares, and their holding period includes that of the old ones. You get the benefit when you sell the replacement shares.

The rule applies across all your accounts and to purchases by your spouse. A purchase in your IRA also triggers it, and in that case the loss is lost permanently, because it cannot be added to a basis inside the IRA (Rev. Rul. 2008-5). Reinvested dividends and automatic investments in the same fund within the window can trigger partial wash sales. Brokers report wash sales only within the same account and for identical securities; you are responsible for everything else. What counts as substantially identical has never been fully defined; two index funds that track different indexes are widely treated as not substantially identical, but there is no official IRS list.

Because netting happens on the return, holding securities at several brokers costs nothing in terms of loss offsetting. The real risk lies elsewhere: a loss you were counting on can disappear through a wash sale that no broker flags. The following model case shows what this costs.

bloecke.titel: Model case 2026 with one investor and two brokers
zeilen: Loss on ETF, held eight months

bloecke.md:
The calculation uses a single filer in the 22% ordinary bracket and the 15% range for long-term gains, without NIIT or state tax.

Long-term: 4,000 − 7,000 + 5,000 = +$2,000. Short-term: −$3,000. Netted against each other, a net capital loss of $1,000 remains. It reduces ordinary income and saves 22% × $1,000 = $220. Nothing is carried forward.

The qualified dividends cost $180 (15%), the interest $176 (22%). In total, the investment items of this year add 180 + 176 − 220 = $136 to the federal tax.

bloecke.titel: The same case with a wash sale
bloecke.md:
The investor buys the same ETF back ten days after the loss sale, because they do not want to be out of the market. The $3,000 short-term loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the new shares.

Now only the long-term net gain of $2,000 remains, taxed at 15% = $300. Together with dividends and interest, the investment items cost 180 + 176 + 300 = $656, which is $520 more than before.

The loss is deferred, not lost, because it raises the basis of the repurchased shares. Had the repurchase taken place in the IRA, the $3,000 would have been lost for good.

schritte.text: Look at the unrealized gains and losses of every taxable account, separately for short-term and long-term lots. Most brokers show this under “unrealized gains/losses” or “tax lots”.

Before selling at a loss, check purchases of the same security in the past 30 days in all accounts, including your IRA, your spouse's accounts, reinvested dividends and automatic investment plans. Pause these for the 30 days after the sale.

schritte.titel: Sell by the last trading day
schritte.text: The trade date counts, so a loss sale must be executed by the last trading day of December. If you want to stay invested, buy a similar fund that tracks a different index instead of the same one.
Enter every sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D, including the wash sale adjustments shown on Form 1099-B. Add any wash sales across accounts that the broker could not see.
Use the capital loss carryover worksheet in the Schedule D instructions to work out what remains, split into short-term and long-term. Keep the worksheet; next year's return starts from it.

bloecke.md: The broker does not carry a loss forward for you. The carryforward exists only on your returns, and you have to bring it from one year to the next yourself. Tax software does this if you use the same program every year; if you switch programs or preparers, enter it manually. An unused capital loss carryforward ends with the taxpayer's death; it cannot be passed on to the heirs. For a married couple filing jointly, the share of the deceased spouse can only be used on the final joint return.

## Carryforward and changing brokers

Because the carryforward is part of your return, it is independent of any broker. Closing an account, transferring securities to another broker or the insolvency of a broker has no effect on it. What a transfer can affect is the basis information: if the new broker does not receive the basis of the transferred lots, the 1099-B for a later sale may show the basis as not reported. You then have to enter it yourself, or you report a gain that does not exist.

## Special cases

- **Worthless securities.** A security that becomes completely worthless is treated as sold on the last day of the tax year in which it became worthless (§ 165(g)). You need evidence that it has no value left, not just that the price has collapsed.
- **Futures and certain options.** Section 1256 contracts, such as regulated futures and broad-based index options, are marked to market at year-end and taxed 60% long-term and 40% short-term, regardless of the holding period. A net loss on them can, on election, be carried back three years against section 1256 gains (§ 1212(c)).
- **Sales to related parties.** A loss on a sale to a family member or a controlled company is not deductible (§ 267).
- **Bad debts.** A private loan that becomes uncollectible is a short-term capital loss (§ 166(d)).
- **Losses inside retirement accounts.** Gains and losses inside a 401(k) or IRA have no tax effect at all; a loss there cannot be deducted.

bloecke.titel: Milestones in the treatment of capital losses
bloecke.unter: The $3,000 limit has not been changed since 1978 and is not adjusted for inflation.

ereignisse.text: The Revenue Act of 1921 introduces the rule that disallows losses on sales followed by a repurchase of the same securities.
Following the Tax Reform Act of 1976, the deduction of net capital losses against other income reaches $3,000 a year.
Revenue Ruling 2008-5 holds that a repurchase in the investor's IRA triggers the wash sale rule, with the loss lost for good.
Brokers begin reporting cost basis and wash sale adjustments to the IRS for stock acquired from 2011, and for fund shares from 2012.
The limit is still $3,000; adjusted for inflation since 1978, it would be several times higher.

bloecke.md:
Without a limit, investors could sell their losing positions, deduct the losses in full from wages taxed at up to 37%, and keep their winners unsold, deferring the tax on gains for as long as they like. The limit restricts this asymmetry between losses, which the investor can realize at will, and gains, which can be deferred.

The amount, however, has been fixed for almost five decades. Measured by the consumer price index, $3,000 in 1978 corresponds to around $14,000 in 2024. In practice, the limit therefore bites much harder today than when it was set. Changing it would require an act of Congress; this lesson describes the law as of 2026.

Foreign taxes withheld on dividends of foreign stocks or of funds that hold them appear in box 7 of Form 1099-DIV. You can claim them as a credit against your US tax. If your creditable foreign taxes are no more than $300 ($600 if married filing jointly) and all come from passive income reported on a 1099, you can claim the credit directly on Form 1040. Otherwise, you need Form 1116, and unused credits can be carried back one year and forward ten years. Foreign taxes withheld inside an IRA or 401(k) cannot be credited at all, which is one reason to hold international stock funds in a taxable account.

- Review your losses in November, not in March. After December 31, a loss can no longer be realized for the current year.
- Watch every purchase of the same security 30 days before and after a loss sale, including dividend reinvestment, your IRA and your spouse's accounts.
- If your gains would be taxed at 0% anyway, harvesting losses saves little; a carryforward is used up automatically against later gains, even at 0%.
- Realize losses only if you would sell anyway or can replace the position with a fund that is not substantially identical. Trading costs and the risk of buying back at a higher price can outweigh the tax saving.

mitnehmen: Capital losses offset capital gains in full; beyond that, only $3,000 a year reduces other income, and the rest is carried forward indefinitely, with no carryback.
Short-term and long-term results are netted separately and then against each other; there are no separate pots for stocks, funds or bonds.
Netting happens on Form 8949 and Schedule D across all brokers, so holding several accounts does not cost anything in loss offsetting.
The wash sale rule disallows a loss if substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale, in any of your accounts, your spouse's or your IRA.
The carryforward exists only on your returns, must be tracked by you and ends with your death.

begriffe.text: Net capital loss that exceeds the $3,000 annual deduction and is carried forward to later years without a time limit (26 U.S.C. § 1212(b)). It keeps its short-term or long-term character and must be used against the first available gains.

Sale at a loss combined with the purchase of substantially identical securities within 30 days before or after (26 U.S.C. § 1091). The loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the new shares; with a repurchase in an IRA, it is lost permanently.
Deliberately realizing losses to offset gains or up to $3,000 of other income, usually while replacing the position with a similar but not substantially identical investment.

Regulated futures contract, broad-based index option or similar contract that is marked to market at year-end and taxed 60% long-term and 40% short-term. Net losses can be carried back three years on election.
